roles.label: Custodian (IT, data custodian or system administrator)

cards.decision: Approve the IS audit charter
cards.why: The charter gives audit its authority, so it is approved above the people audited: by the audit committee, for the board.
cards.auditor_move: The CAE drafts the charter; if the CIO approved it, report that first.

cards.decision: Approve the risk-based annual audit plan
cards.why: The audit committee approves the plan and its resources, so the managers being audited cannot steer what gets audited.
cards.auditor_move: When risk changes, re-rank the plan and seek committee approval again.

cards.decision: Receive the formal IS audit report
cards.why: The report goes to the governance body audit reports to; managers who must fix the issues get copies.
cards.auditor_move: Never address it to the CISO who will fix the finding.

cards.decision: Review the audit function's budget and staffing
cards.why: Committee review of audit's resources stops the managers being audited from starving the function of people or money.

cards.decision: Oversee the chief audit executive as audit's functional reporting line
cards.why: Functional reporting to the audit committee protects independence; a senior executive handles only day-to-day administration.

cards.decision: Agree on the scope of audit's external quality assessment and receive its results
cards.why: The CAE agrees on the assessor's scope and independence with the audit committee, then reports the results and actions to it.

cards.decision: Set the enterprise's risk appetite
cards.why: Appetite is the board's broad stance on how much risk to take; management sets measurable limits within it.

cards.decision: Approve keeping a risk that exceeds appetite
cards.why: Above appetite, risk is treated until it fits. Only the board, which set the appetite, can approve an exception.
cards.auditor_move: Report the excess; recommend treatment or a board-approved exception.

cards.decision: Approve the information security strategy
cards.why: The board approves the security strategy and sets acceptable information risk; the CISO designs and runs the program.

cards.decision: Approve the enterprise AI policy and AI risk appetite
cards.why: AI is governed like any high-impact process: a board-approved policy and appetite, then a named business owner per model.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend fixing governance gaps before any technical tuning.

cards.decision: Approve the risk policy that sets roles and accountability for risk management
cards.why: A board-approved risk policy gives the program its appetite, roles and accountability; consultants can help build it but never own it.

cards.decision: Set the enterprise's IT direction and IT risk limits
cards.why: Setting direction and risk limits is governance; executives then plan and run IT, and the steering committee then ranks projects within it.

cards.decision: Decide a tolerance breach that is still within appetite
cards.why: Tolerance breaches escalate to senior management to decide; the appetite itself stays the board's call.

cards.decision: Approve the business impact analysis (BIA) results
cards.why: The BIA is a business document; senior management approves it before recovery strategies are chosen or funded.
cards.auditor_move: Evaluate the method and evidence; never set criticality yourself.

cards.decision: Authorize a penetration test in writing
cards.why: Written management authorization, scope and rules of engagement come first; they separate a lawful test from an attack.

cards.decision: Accredit a new system, accepting its residual risk to operate
cards.why: Accreditation is a management decision by an authorized senior official; testers only certify that controls meet requirements.
cards.auditor_move: Report the gaps; approving or blocking go-live would impair independence.

cards.decision: Set the enterprise sourcing strategy for core systems
cards.why: Outsourcing moves the work, never the accountability. Management makes the sourcing call after weighing risks beyond cost.
cards.auditor_move: Check the analysis covers data location, lost knowledge and exit, then leave the choice to management.

cards.decision: Commit sponsorship and resources to launch the BCP program
cards.why: Senior management commitment and an approved policy start the program and set its scope, objectives and accountabilities.

cards.decision: Approve the incident response plan
cards.why: The plan draws its authority from management approval and alignment with security policy and risk, before procedures are refined.
cards.auditor_move: Check the plan's approval before its details.

cards.decision: Approve a scope and budget change beyond the project manager's limits
cards.why: The steering committee decides what exceeds the project manager's limits; its members must be able to commit money and people.

cards.decision: Rank competing IT projects and settle resource conflicts
cards.why: The IT steering committee, a management body, prioritizes projects; the board-level IT strategy committee only advises on direction.

cards.decision: Decide a go-live deviation from agreed UAT exit criteria
cards.why: When UAT misses its exit criteria, go-live is deferred; any deviation is decided and documented by the steering committee.
cards.auditor_move: Report the gap against the agreed criteria; do not block go-live.

cards.decision: Confirm the development method before approving the project plan
cards.why: The method shapes cost, control and evidence, so the steering committee confirms it before approving the plan.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend the method that fits the requirements; the committee decides.

cards.decision: Choose build, buy or subscribe for an approved project at its feasibility gate
cards.why: The steering committee decides once a total cost comparison, including exit costs and requirements fit, is on the table.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend a full cost-of-ownership comparison before the decision.

cards.decision: Approve a rebaselined plan after a major scope change
cards.why: Scope changes need impact analysis first; the steering committee approves them after seeing the cost and schedule impact.
cards.auditor_move: Check the minutes show the impact was seen before approval.

cards.decision: Classify the loyalty-program member data
cards.why: The owner knows the data's business value and legal duties, so the owner assigns the classification level.
cards.auditor_move: No named owner? Recommend naming one before any labeling starts.

cards.decision: Approve a request to view customer loan applications
cards.why: The data owner approves access against business need; custodians then grant it as directed.

cards.decision: Approve the rules that map legacy fields into a new system
cards.why: Mapping decides what converted data means to the business, so the data owner approves it, not IT alone.

cards.decision: Lower a report's classification so it can be shared more widely
cards.why: Only the data owner sets or changes a level; users follow the label and ask the owner when it looks wrong.

cards.decision: Approve which fields an analysts' database view will show
cards.why: The owner decides what the view exposes; the database administrator builds and grants it under change control.

cards.decision: Approve the risk assessment before moving patient records to a public cloud
cards.why: The data owner stays accountable for the records wherever they sit, so the owner approves the move's risk assessment.

cards.decision: Approve using a production data extract in a test environment
cards.why: Test data is controlled like any sensitive data set: owner approval, restricted access, masking and deletion after testing.

cards.decision: Run nightly backups of loan files as the owner directs
cards.why: Custodians store and protect data as the owner directs; how backups are run is a custodian task.

cards.decision: Configure access rights and encryption to match a data set's classification
cards.why: Custodians, such as system and database administrators, apply the controls the owner's classification requires.

cards.decision: Grant an approved database view to analysts under change control
cards.why: The database administrator builds and grants the view; the data owner has already decided what it may show.

cards.decision: Remove access rights the business owner did not recertify
cards.why: Owners judge business need; IT carries out the removals, because it administers the accounts.

cards.decision: Store and protect a client's records as a contracted cloud provider
cards.why: A provider that stores data is a custodian under contract; ownership and accountability stay with the business.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend naming a business owner, with the provider as custodian.

cards.decision: Purge retired laptop drives with a verified secure-erase command
cards.why: IT, as custodian, sanitizes media by the method the data's sensitivity requires and records each drive on a certificate.

cards.decision: Disable vendor default administrator accounts on new servers
cards.why: Custodians harden systems to the approved baseline; the infrastructure team owns fixing the drift.

cards.decision: Accept a residual risk in the claims process that sits within tolerance
cards.why: Authority rises with risk: owners accept within tolerance, senior management decides breaches, and the board decides above appetite.
cards.auditor_move: Verify a documented, dated acceptance; never accept it yourself.

cards.decision: Accept the residual risk of a dated baseline exception for a server
cards.why: A baseline gap needs a formal exception: documented, risk-accepted by the asset owner, with an expiry date and compensating control.
cards.auditor_move: Test that the compensating control actually operates.

cards.decision: Accept a 30-day patch delay, within tolerance, with compensating controls
cards.why: When a patch must wait, the business owner accepts the time-bound risk; internal acceptance cannot waive a regulator's deadline.

cards.decision: Approve user acceptance testing (UAT) results against agreed criteria
cards.why: UAT is the business's acceptance: the business owner, not the developers, approves results against criteria agreed in advance.

cards.decision: Commit to the action, owner and due date for an audit finding
cards.why: Management owns remediation and gives the planned action, owner and date; the auditor recommends and later verifies.
cards.auditor_move: Record management's response beside the finding, then follow up by risk.

cards.decision: Run a control self-assessment of the process's own controls
cards.why: In a CSA, process owners and staff evaluate their own controls; audit may facilitate, and still tests key controls itself.

cards.decision: Approve system requirements as the design baseline
cards.why: Business owners approve the requirements, which become the baseline for design, build and testing.
cards.auditor_move: Check traceability from each requirement to a test.

cards.decision: Test management's continuous monitoring before relying on it
cards.why: Monitoring is a management control; the auditor tests that it works, then adjusts other testing. Never rely on it untested.

cards.decision: Evaluate the BIA method and the evidence behind its ratings
cards.why: The auditor evaluates method and evidence and advises, but never sets criticality; owners and senior management do.

cards.decision: Verify that agreed remediation actions were implemented and work
cards.why: Follow-up independently tests each action, scaled to risk; management's word that it is fixed is not evidence.

cards.decision: Advise on control requirements during system design
cards.why: Early advice is expected and cheapest; independence comes from not designing, building or approving the system.

cards.decision: Design and run continuous auditing routines
cards.why: Continuous auditing is built and run by the audit function for independent assurance; continuous monitoring belongs to management.

cards.decision: Disclose a past role in the audited system before fieldwork
cards.why: The auditor discloses the threat before work starts; audit management then judges it and reassigns or adds safeguards.

cards.decision: Design the classification scheme and monitor compliance with it
cards.why: Security designs the scheme, advises and monitors, but does not own business data. Owners classify; custodians implement.

cards.decision: Design and run the information security program
cards.why: The CISO designs and runs the program and reports to senior management; accountability stays with the board and senior management.

cards.decision: Receive laptop-encryption compliance reports as the security policy owner
cards.why: Compliance monitoring reports gaps to the policy owner, here the CISO, who keeps the policy current and enforced.

cards.decision: Monitor and challenge IT operations' handling of security risk
cards.why: Security is a second-line function: it sets frameworks, monitors and challenges the first line, but it is not independent assurance.

cards.decision: Own, test and retire SIEM correlation rules
cards.why: Detection decays unless someone owns it; security operations treats rules as code, tests them with simulated attacks and retires stale ones.

cards.decision: Approve a high-risk production change after CAB review
cards.why: The change advisory board (CAB) reviews higher-risk changes and advises; the change authority approves.
cards.auditor_move: Trace changes found in production back to approved requests.

cards.decision: Approve deploying a peer-reviewed firewall rule change to production
cards.why: Firewall rules are production changes: peer review checks the rule against default-deny, then the change authority approves it.

cards.decision: Approve a change to the production job schedule
cards.why: Schedulers do not approve their own production schedule changes; independent approval through change control keeps duties separate.

cards.decision: Approve releasing a retrained machine learning model to production
cards.why: A model is a controlled component: validated independently, then released through normal change control with a tested way back.

cards.decision: Approve the production change that decommissions a legacy server
cards.why: Retirement is a change like any other: requested, assessed for impact on dependent systems, approved and recorded.

cards.decision: Ransomware starts encrypting shared files during fieldwork. First move: isolate the host.
cards.why: Containment is the response team's job under management's authority; the auditor never touches the affected system.
cards.auditor_move: Alert the incident manager at once; evaluate the response afterward.

cards.decision: Server restarts fail and mining malware is found. First: contain it and remove the foothold.
cards.why: Security incidents differ from outages: independent security responders contain and eradicate before service is restored.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend that triage flag signs of compromise and route them to security.

cards.decision: A certificate authority never used before issued a certificate for the checkout domain. First: request revocation.
cards.why: A rogue certificate must lose trust at once; the security team requests revocation and investigates instead of waiting for misuse.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend revoking now; waiting for misuse is not a control.

cards.decision: The IT director asks audit to sign off an above-appetite risk. First: decline and report it.
cards.why: Accepting risk is a management role that would impair independence; the auditor reports and recommends treatment or a board exception.

cards.decision: A buyer approves invoices for vendors sharing a staff home address. First: document and escalate to the CAE.
cards.why: The auditor records the facts, secures the logs and escalates under the fraud procedure; authorized investigators decide what follows.
cards.auditor_move: Never confront the buyer or widen the sample before escalating.

cards.decision: A former vendor still receives a nightly loyalty-data export. First: recommend suspending it and report the exposure.
cards.why: With no business approval for the job, the auditor recommends closing the bypass at once and reports to the privacy officer, who decides.

cards.decision: Fraud red flags point at senior management, with a regulator deadline. First: receive the escalation.
cards.why: When management may be implicated, escalate promptly above it, to the audit committee and legal counsel.
cards.auditor_move: Preserve the evidence with a chain of custody; do not investigate alone.

cards.decision: The CFO presses the CAE a third time to drop a planned audit. First: receive the escalation.
cards.why: The audit committee protects audit independence, so repeated management pressure goes to it once the CAE has declined.
cards.auditor_move: Decline the first request and explain the risk rating.

cards.decision: A critical finding with a legal deadline surfaces between meetings. First: receive it now.
cards.why: Severity sets the timing: critical issues go to the audit committee chair at once, not at the next scheduled meeting.

cards.decision: A department head offers to sign off a patient-data risk above appetite. First: direct its treatment.
cards.why: The department head lacks authority; senior management directs treatment, and only the board could approve keeping the excess.
cards.auditor_move: Report that the risk exceeds appetite and recommend escalation.

cards.decision: The revenue director calls an overdue refund-approval fix 'not worth fixing', though the risk exceeds appetite. First escalation point?
cards.why: The CAE raises above-appetite accepted risk with senior management first, then with the audit committee.
cards.auditor_move: Confirm each action's status and report the overdue items.

cards.decision: End-of-support servers cannot be replaced in time, and the risk exceeds appetite. Approve keeping them.
cards.why: Above appetite, the risk must be treated; only a board-approved exception can keep it until the servers are replaced.
cards.auditor_move: Verify interim controls and a funded, dated replacement plan.

cards.decision: Projected losses from an outage would exceed the enterprise's risk capacity. First: decide, outside the normal cycle, how much loss the enterprise will carry.
cards.why: Breaching risk capacity puts survival at stake, so the board acts at once rather than waiting for the normal cycle.

cards.decision: The vendor asks for six more weeks, beyond the project manager's authority. First: decide the extension.
cards.why: Issues beyond the project manager's limits go to the steering committee, whose members can commit money and people.
cards.auditor_move: Confirm the minutes record a decision.

cards.decision: An emergency fix went live overnight with no prior approval. Next working day: review and approve it.
cards.why: Urgency changes the route, not the need: emergency changes get independent review and approval soon after implementation.

cards.decision: A pricing change arrives marked 'tested' with no results attached. First: withhold approval.
cards.why: The change authority approves only on attached evidence; the author's word is not evidence.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend the pipeline block deployment until test evidence is attached.

cards.decision: IT says the hosting vendor now owns migrated student records. Who stays accountable for them?
cards.why: Ownership follows business accountability, not storage location; outsourcing creates a custodian, never a new owner.

cards.decision: Conversion reconciliation is done the day before go-live. Sign off acceptance of the converted data.
cards.why: The data owner reviews the reconciliation results and accepts the converted data; IT runs the load but cannot accept it.
cards.auditor_move: Recommend full count-and-total reconciliation, not spot checks.

cards.decision: A bad script overwrote 40,000 addresses. Choose between restore paths that trade data loss against time.
cards.why: When recovery paths trade data loss against time, the data owner decides, because the business bears the impact.
cards.auditor_move: Report each path's impact; leave the choice to the owner.

cards.decision: The owner has chosen the recovery path after a bad script. Run the point-in-time restore.
cards.why: The database administrator restores the backup, rolls the log forward and verifies; the data owner already chose the path.

cards.decision: Leavers' accounts are still active months after they left. First: disable them.
cards.why: IT administers accounts, so it disables orphan accounts at once and checks them for misuse; the HR feed is fixed next.

cards.decision: A continuous-auditing alert flags rapid cashier voids at night. First: the manager who runs the cashier process decides whether to freeze the cashier's till access.
cards.why: Operational responses, such as freezing an account, belong to the manager with authority to act, not to audit.
cards.auditor_move: Call the manager with authority and preserve the evidence.
